topics.name: Matter and its States
topics.summary: Solids, liquids and gases, and what happens at the changes between them.

objectives.text: Describe the arrangement of particles in solids, liquids and gases.
Explain why a gas fills its container but a solid does not.

keyTerms.definition: The tiny unit all matter is made of, far too small to see.
Solid, liquid or gas — determined by how the particles are arranged and how they move.
The amount of space something takes up.
To squeeze into a smaller volume. Possible for gases, barely possible for solids and liquids.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
Ice, water and steam are the same substance. What makes them behave so differently is not what they are made of, but how their particles are arranged.

By the end you will be able to:

• describe how particles sit and move in a solid, a liquid and a gas
• explain why each state keeps or loses its shape and volume
• use the particle model to predict how a substance will behave

sections.heading: Particles and arrangement
sections.body:
All matter is made of tiny particles. What makes a solid different from a liquid or a gas is not the particles themselves but how they are arranged and how freely they move. In a solid they are packed closely in a fixed pattern and can only vibrate. In a liquid they are still close together but can slide past one another. In a gas they are far apart and move quickly in all directions.

This is the key idea of the whole topic: the particles in ice, water and steam are identical. Heating does not change the particles. It gives them more energy, so they move more and hold their arrangement less.

    SOLID   ●●●●   fixed pattern, vibrating on the spot
    LIQUID  ●● ●●  close but sliding past each other
    GAS     ●   ●  far apart, moving fast in all directions

sections.heading: Shape and volume
sections.body:
Because solid particles hold their positions, a solid keeps its own shape and volume. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container, since its particles can flow. A gas keeps neither — its particles spread out until they fill whatever space they are given.

That last point is what makes a gas fill its container. There is nothing holding the particles together, so they simply keep moving until the walls stop them.

It also explains compression. A gas has large gaps between particles, so it can be squeezed into a smaller volume. A solid or liquid has almost no gaps, which is why you cannot squash a bottle of water.
sections.example:
Water shows all three. Ice holds its shape. Liquid water takes the shape of the cup. Steam spreads through the whole kitchen.

                shape?      volume?
    solid       keeps       keeps
    liquid      takes       keeps
    gas         takes       takes

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body:
A sealed syringe contains air. You push the plunger in. Then you fill the same syringe with water and try again.

(a) What happens with the air?

    The plunger moves in a long way. Gas particles are far apart, so there is
    space for them to be pushed closer together.

(b) What happens with the water?

    The plunger barely moves. Liquid particles are already touching, so there
    is almost no space to remove.

(c) What does this tell you?

    The difference is not the particles but the GAPS between them. Gases
    compress because they are mostly empty space; liquids do not because they
    are not.

(d) Predict: would a block of wood compress?

    No. Its particles are packed in a fixed pattern with no gaps to close —
    even less free space than a liquid.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.body:
**Thinking the particles themselves change.** The particles in ice and steam are exactly the same. Only their arrangement and energy differ.

**Saying a gas has no volume.** A gas takes the volume of its container. It does not lack volume; it lacks a fixed one.

**Confusing "takes the shape" with "keeps the volume".** A liquid does both at once: it takes the container's shape while keeping its own volume.

**Thinking particles in a solid are still.** They vibrate. They simply cannot leave their positions.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. In which state are particles packed in a fixed pattern?

2. Why does a gas fill its whole container?

3. Which state keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container?

4. Explain why air can be compressed in a syringe but water cannot.

5. A substance keeps its volume but flows into the shape of its jar. Which state is it?

6. Ice, water and steam are the same substance. What is different about them?

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• All matter is made of particles; the state depends on their arrangement and movement.
• Solid: fixed pattern, vibrating. Keeps shape and volume.
• Liquid: close but sliding. Takes shape, keeps volume.
• Gas: far apart, fast. Takes both shape and volume.
• Gases compress because of the gaps between particles; solids and liquids have almost none.

questions.question: In which state of matter are the particles packed closely in a fixed pattern?
questions.explanation: In a solid the particles hold fixed positions and can only vibrate. That is why a solid keeps its own shape.

questions.question: Why does a gas fill its whole container?
options: Its particles are heavier than liquid particles
Its particles are far apart and move freely in all directions
Its particles are joined in a fixed pattern
questions.explanation: Gas particles are widely spaced and move quickly in every direction, so they spread out until they occupy the whole space available.

questions.question: Which state keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container?
questions.explanation: Liquid particles stay close together, so the volume is fixed, but they slide past one another, so the shape changes to fit the container.
